heuristics.rule: Don't return to search — return to start
heuristics.condition: When planning a staged return to your home country
heuristics.action: Interview for home-country roles while still employed in the US, accept the offer before giving US notice, and negotiate a start date that allows unvested equity to vest
heuristics.because: Returning without employment puts you in a weak negotiating position — you're a returnee without current US anchor, under implicit time pressure, and perceived as less valuable than someone actively employed

heuristics.rule: Define pre-committed return conditions before they can shift forward
heuristics.condition: When you tell yourself 'I'll return eventually, after X'
heuristics.action: Write down specific, measurable milestones (title, liquid savings, named contacts, specific role) and treat them as binding triggers rather than aspirational targets
heuristics.because: Vague future conditions shift indefinitely — green card timelines extend, savings targets rise, and the person wakes up at 45 having never made a conscious choice to stay

heuristics.rule: Build 3–5 specific home-country relationships who know your work quality before returning
heuristics.condition: When preparing for a staged return in any field
heuristics.action: Deliberately cultivate home-country network while still in the US through advising, conferences, consulting engagements, and LinkedIn thought leadership — not after arrival
heuristics.because: Returnees with a strong home-country network find roles in 1–3 months; those without one take 6–18 months and often return to the US in frustration

heuristics.rule: Frame return as a phase with evaluation conditions, not a permanent decision
heuristics.condition: When the psychological block 'if I return I can never come back' is delaying action
heuristics.action: Set a 2–3 year evaluation window with explicit criteria for whether the phase is working, and maintain awareness of re-entry options (remote work, third-country, return to US)
heuristics.because: Treating return as permanent causes either indefinite delay or desperate rushing before readiness; neither is optimal and re-entry options for US-experienced professionals are more available than assumed

heuristics.rule: Wait for a major vesting event before departing
heuristics.condition: When you have unvested equity at a US company and a return offer in hand
heuristics.action: Negotiate your home-country start date to allow the vesting event to complete before giving US notice
heuristics.because: Unvested equity is a concrete financial asset that is permanently forfeited on early departure — it is a quantifiable cost of unplanned timing

heuristics.rule: For academia, longer US tenure directly increases home-country negotiating leverage
heuristics.condition: When an academic is evaluating how long to stay in the US before returning
heuristics.action: Stay long enough to accumulate publications and reputation because home-country universities are specifically recruiting for that credential
heuristics.because: The staged return is best aligned with academia — the longer the stay with demonstrated output, the stronger the startup fund, salary supplement, and housing package you can negotiate on return

decision_factors.factor: Liquid savings threshold (separate from retirement accounts)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines financial resilience during the transition — covers career gap, return costs, housing downpayment, and time to find the right role without desperation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Classify yourself by risk profile: conservative ($300K–$500K), moderate ($150K–$250K), aggressive ($80K–$120K); aggressive only valid if family housing available, no children, partner already employed in home country, and specific offer in hand

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines speed and quality of role acquisition on return — the difference between 1–3 months and 6–18 months of job search, and whether you return to a role or return to frustration
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count the number of specific individuals in your target home city who know your work quality and can hire or refer you; target minimum of 3–5 such relationships built before departure

decision_factors.factor: Title and scope level at time of return
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines the quality of roles available in the home country and your credibility as a returnee — home-country employers benchmark against US credentials
decision_factors.how_to_assess: For tech: Senior/Staff or above (L5/L6 equivalent); for finance: VP or MD level; for academia: PhD plus postdoc with publications; assess whether current trajectory reaches target within 3–7 years

decision_factors.factor: Specific role or founding plan identified before departure
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The presence or absence of a specific role before leaving is the single biggest determinant of transition success — it eliminates the weak-position job search scenario
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Is there a concrete offer letter, a founding plan with committed LPs, or a named professorship offer? If not, the return trigger has not been met regardless of other milestones

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Dual-income families and those with partners who have independent career trajectories have different financial thresholds and must have both careers mapped before departure
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Has the partner identified specific home-country career paths? Are both people's professional networks and role pipelines ready simultaneously? Misalignment here can cause one partner to sacrifice career continuity

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Represents a concrete, time-sensitive financial asset that is forfeited if departure timing is not planned around vesting events
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Pull the vesting schedule and calculate the dollar value of unvested equity at various departure dates; factor this into negotiating home-country start dates

decision_factors.why_it_matters: In fields like medicine, US credentials do not automatically transfer — clinical licensing in the home country may take 2–3 additional years, fundamentally changing the return timeline and viable return paths
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research the specific licensing pathway in your field in your target country; determine whether clinical, research, industry, or administrative tracks are viable and on what timeline

decision_factors.factor: Whether the urgency is family-driven versus financially optimal
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Family-driven urgency (eldercare crisis, partner preference) is a legitimate override of financial milestones; absence of family urgency means financial thresholds should be honored before returning
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Explicitly identify whether the pressure to return comes from a concrete family need or from generalized emotional pull; if the latter, assess whether milestones are actually met

decision_factors.factor: Advisory or consulting engagements with home-country companies while in the US
decision_factors.why_it_matters: These serve dual purpose: verifying that the home-country market is as expected, and building the network credentialing required for fast role acquisition on return
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Have you completed 1–2 paid or advisory engagements with home-country companies? Have these relationships progressed to the point of hire-or-refer capability?

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The financial gap between US and home-country compensation varies enormously by field — for US-trained physicians it is so severe that many choose not to return to clinical practice at all
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research actual compensation data for equivalent roles in your target city; calculate the long-term compounding impact of the salary differential; distinguish between fields where gap closes (tech, finance) versus remains permanent (clinical medicine)

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Returning before financial milestones are met
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You enter the home-country job market from a position of implicit time pressure and financial stress, which weakens negotiating leverage and increases the probability of accepting a suboptimal role just to generate income
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Primary earners with children or significant financial obligations who underestimated transition costs and career gap duration

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The conditions for return silently shift forward — each milestone gets replaced by a higher one, and the decision calcifies into a de facto permanent stay that was never consciously chosen
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals in their 30s who feel no acute pressure to decide, particularly those on green card tracks where immigration status makes staying feel lower friction

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Returning to search rather than returning to start
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You lose the negotiating power of current US employment and the US anchor that signals ongoing relevance to home-country employers; the job search takes 6–18 months instead of 1–3, and often ends in returning to the US in frustration
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals who feel discomfort interviewing while employed and treat that discomfort as a reason to wait until after departure to begin the search

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Treating return as permanent and irreversible
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The psychological weight of perceived permanence causes either indefinite delay (never returning) or panic-driven premature return; both outcomes are worse than treating return as a phase
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals who have built strong US identities and social networks and experience the decision as an all-or-nothing identity choice rather than a career phase decision

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Focusing staged return planning on savings and title while ignoring network
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You arrive with financial cushion and impressive credentials but no one in the home city who can move quickly to hire you — the credential is visible but unverifiable to local employers without a trusted intermediary
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Analytically oriented professionals who optimize for quantifiable metrics (savings, level, equity) and underweight relationship-building, which feels unquantifiable

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Returning to clinical medicine in the home country after US training
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Income compression from US physician to home-country physician compensation is so severe that the financial model of staged return breaks down — the savings built in the US may never be replicated through home-country clinical earnings
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: US-trained physicians who assumed home-country clinical practice would offer a comparable professional and financial trajectory to US practice

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Aligning only one partner's career before departure
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The partner without a clear home-country career path faces career discontinuity, credential re-establishment costs, and possible income loss — which can undermine household financial stability and create relationship strain during an already high-stress transition
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Couples where one partner drives the return decision and the other's career is treated as secondary or assumed to 'figure itself out'

failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The person sets a future milestone (green card, 5 years, $X savings) that functions as a psychological placeholder rather than a binding commitment; as each milestone approaches, a new reason to extend emerges and the condition shifts forward
failure_patterns.consequence: The person reaches their mid-40s having never made a conscious decision to stay — they stayed by default, not by choice, and often experience this as a significant loss of agency
warning_signs: The return timeline has already shifted once or more in the past
The person cannot name specific, measurable milestones — only vague conditions like 'when things are more stable'

failure_patterns.pattern: Returning without a home-country network and treating job search as something to do after arrival
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Network-building requires sustained effort with delayed payoff and feels awkward to prioritize while building a US career; professionals assume their credentials will speak for themselves in the home-country market
failure_patterns.consequence: 6–18 month job search after return, financial depletion of the savings buffer, psychological demoralization, and frequent reversal of the return decision — flying back to the US having never successfully launched
warning_signs: Cannot name 3–5 specific people in their target home city who know their work quality
Has not done any advisory, consulting, or speaking engagements connected to the home-country market

failure_patterns.pattern: Resigning before securing a home-country role
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Interviewing while employed feels uncomfortable or disloyal; the person believes it is more honest or less complicated to quit first, then search; or they are reacting to a US workplace frustration impulsively
failure_patterns.consequence: Negotiating leverage is lost — you are perceived as available rather than recruited; time pressure from diminishing savings forces acceptance of suboptimal offers; the US-anchor signal (currently employed at US company) disappears
warning_signs: Person has announced departure plans internally before a home-country offer is in hand
Person expresses discomfort with the idea of interviewing while still employed as a reason to delay the search

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating the return decision as permanently binary
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The cultural and emotional weight of 'going home' or 'leaving the US' activates identity-level thinking; the person frames it as a final, irreversible choice rather than a career phase with evaluation conditions
failure_patterns.consequence: Either permanent delay (the decision is too weighty to make, so it is never made) or premature rushed return (the person forces the decision to relieve the psychological burden, before milestones are met)
warning_signs: Person says 'if I go back, I can never return to the US'
Person describes the decision in identity terms ('I would be giving up my life here') rather than career-phase terms

failure_patterns.pattern: Optimizing for savings and title while neglecting network credentialing
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Savings and titles are quantifiable and easy to track; network quality is subjective, requires vulnerability, and the payoff is invisible until the moment of return job search
failure_patterns.consequence: Arrives in home country with strong financial position and impressive resume but no warm introductions to hiring decision-makers; transition takes far longer than planned and erodes the financial cushion that was supposed to provide runway
warning_signs: Staged return plan lists savings targets and title milestones but no network-building activities
Has not attended a single professional conference or event in their home country in the past 2 years

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you name 3–5 specific people in your target home city who know your work quality and could hire or refer you today?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether network credentialing has been done — the most commonly neglected milestone that determines transition speed and quality
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have any of these relationships progressed to a concrete conversation about a role or engagement in the past 12 months?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What specific mechanisms are you using to build these relationships before departure — advising, conferences, consulting, LinkedIn?

diagnostic_questions.question: What are your exact return conditions, and have any of them shifted in the past 2 years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has binding pre-committed milestones or shifting placeholders; past shifts are the strongest predictor of future shifts
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What caused the shift, and what mechanism will prevent the new conditions from shifting again?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Are the conditions specific and measurable (title, dollar amount, named contacts, specific role) or vague ('when things settle down', 'after a few more years')?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a specific role, offer, or founding plan identified in the home country — not a general intention to search after arrival?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is planning to return to start or return to search — the single biggest determinant of transition success
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is this offer in hand, or is it a conversation in progress? Have you negotiated a start date that allows your US equity to vest?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What is the timeline for developing a specific role pipeline before departure, and are you interviewing for home-country roles while still employed?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your liquid savings position, separate from retirement accounts, and which risk profile does it put you in?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the financial milestone has been met and which risk category applies — conservative, moderate, or aggressive — relative to the person's specific obligations (children, primary earner status, family support availability)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Do you have children or are you the primary earner? If so, the conservative threshold ($300K–$500K) likely applies rather than the moderate or aggressive ones.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the urgency to return family-driven (eldercare, partner preference) or financially motivated? If not family-driven, the financial milestone should be honored before departure.

diagnostic_questions.question: Has your partner identified specific career paths in the home country, or is their career being treated as something that will figure itself out after arrival?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether dual-career alignment has been done — a commonly overlooked milestone that can undermine household financial stability and relationship quality during transition
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are both career pipelines at roughly the same stage of readiness, or is one partner significantly further along than the other?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the partner's career in a field with clear home-country equivalents, or does it require licensing, credential re-establishment, or significant market research before a viable path is clear?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your unvested equity position, and have you factored the vesting schedule into your departure timing?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether a concrete, time-sensitive financial asset is being considered in the return timing — a commonly forfeited value that is quantifiable and avoidable
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Can you negotiate a home-country start date that allows the major vesting event to complete before you give US notice?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Have you calculated the dollar value of equity that would be forfeited at your current planned departure date versus a date timed to a vesting event?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you believe that returning to your home country is a permanent, irreversible decision?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is in binary/identity-level thinking that will cause either indefinite delay or premature rushed return
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What specifically makes you believe re-entry to the US would not be possible — have you researched remote work options, third-country paths, or US re-entry timelines for returning professionals?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Have you set a 2–3 year evaluation window with explicit criteria for assessing whether the return phase is working?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the urgency to return driven by a concrete family need (eldercare crisis, partner's strong preference) or by generalized emotional pull?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether a legitimate override of financial milestones is present, or whether the person is rationalizing an emotionally-driven departure before readiness
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Has the family need been scoped — is this a defined crisis with a likely resolution timeline, or an ongoing structural obligation that will not diminish after return?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Given the absence of acute family urgency, are your financial, network, and role milestones fully met? If not, what is the cost of waiting until they are?

industry_realities.common_belief: Staged return means staying longer in the US — it is about accumulating more time before leaving
industry_realities.actual_reality: Staged return is about defining clear, pre-committed, measurable conditions for return and holding to them — the point is to avoid indefinite delay, not to justify more time in the US
industry_realities.implication: If you are using 'staged return' as a label for an unplanned open-ended stay, you are not doing a staged return — you are defaulting to indefinite stay with a more comfortable name for it

industry_realities.common_belief: Your US credentials and resume will be recognized and valued by home-country employers without additional relationship-building
industry_realities.actual_reality: Credentials are visible but unverifiable without trusted intermediaries; the home-country employer market is relationship-driven and a strong resume from a FAANG company does not substitute for a warm introduction from someone who knows your work quality
industry_realities.implication: Network credentialing — building 3–5 specific relationships who can hire or refer you — must be treated as a first-order milestone alongside savings and title, not an afterthought

industry_realities.common_belief: Once you return to your home country, returning to the US is extremely difficult or impossible
industry_realities.actual_reality: Realistic re-entry options include remote work for US companies (normalized post-COVID), US companies expanding into your home country, direct US return within 5–7 years while experience is fresh, and third-country intermediary options (Singapore, Canada, UK)
industry_realities.implication: The mental model of permanence is a cognitive distortion that leads to suboptimal decisions at both ends — either indefinite delay or premature rushed return; frame it as a phase with evaluation conditions instead

industry_realities.common_belief: The most important milestones before returning are savings and professional title
industry_realities.actual_reality: Network is the most underrated milestone — the person who returns with strong home-country relationships finds a role in 1–3 months; the person without them takes 6–18 months and often ends up back in the US
industry_realities.implication: Deliberate network-building while still in the US — advising, conferences, consulting — should begin 2–3 years before planned return, not after arrival

industry_realities.common_belief: US-trained physicians can return to clinical practice in their home country with the same career and financial trajectory they would have had staying in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: Income compression from US physician to home-country physician is so severe that many US-trained physicians choose not to return to clinical practice at all; viable return paths are typically research/academic, industry/medtech, or administration
industry_realities.implication: Medicine requires field-specific staged return planning that accounts for licensing complexity and income compression — a generic financial milestone framework does not apply

industry_realities.common_belief: It is more honest or straightforward to quit your US job before beginning the home-country job search
industry_realities.actual_reality: Resigning before securing a home-country role eliminates your negotiating leverage, removes the US-anchor signal that home-country employers value, and puts you under implicit time pressure that forces acceptance of suboptimal offers
industry_realities.implication: The discomfort of interviewing while employed is real but the cost of the alternative is significantly higher — interview for home-country roles while still employed, accept before giving notice, and negotiate start dates around vesting events

industry_realities.common_belief: Academia is a difficult field for staged return because US tenure-track positions are hard to leave
industry_realities.actual_reality: Academia is the field where staged return is best aligned — home-country universities (through programs like Thousand Talents, Excellent Young Scientists Fund) are specifically recruiting for US research positions, and longer US tenure with more publications directly increases negotiating power for startup funds, salary supplements, and housing packages
industry_realities.implication: Academic professionals should view their US position as an asset that appreciates over time for home-country negotiation purposes — staying longer with continued publication output translates directly into better return offers

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Sets vague, shifting conditions ('after I get my green card,' 'after 5 more years,' 'after I save enough') that function as emotional placeholders rather than binding commitments
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Defines specific, measurable, pre-committed milestones (exact title level, exact dollar amount of liquid savings, named contacts, specific role or offer) and treats them as triggers rather than targets
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Vague conditions shift indefinitely and result in a de facto permanent stay that was never consciously chosen; specific conditions create a decision architecture that forces a real choice

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Sequencing of job search relative to departure
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Plans to return first, then begin the home-country job search from home — treating the search as something that happens after the decision is made
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Interviews for home-country roles while still employed in the US, accepts the offer before giving notice, and negotiates start dates to protect unvested equity
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The junior approach forfeits negotiating leverage, removes the US-anchor signal, and introduces time pressure; the senior approach returns from strength rather than desperation

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Which milestones get prioritized in return planning
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses on quantifiable metrics — savings balance and job title — because they are easy to track, while treating network-building as a vague future task
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats network credentialing as a first-order milestone alongside savings and title, begins deliberate home-country relationship cultivation 2–3 years before planned return
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Arriving with strong financials and credentials but no warm introductions leads to 6–18 month job searches that deplete the financial cushion and often end in return to the US

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How the return decision is framed cognitively
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Frames return as a permanent, identity-level, binary choice — 'leaving the US forever' versus 'staying' — which triggers either indefinite avoidance or panic-driven premature action
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Frames return as a career phase with a defined evaluation window (2–3 years), explicit criteria for assessing whether the phase is working, and awareness of re-entry options
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Binary framing produces suboptimal decisions at both ends; phase framing enables deliberate, reversible action with evaluation built in

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Applies a generic framework (save money, reach a title, then return) without accounting for field-specific constraints like licensing, income compression, or credential recruitment programs
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Understands the specific return pathway relevant to their field — licensing requirements, which institutions recruit for US credentials, which track (clinical, research, industry, academic) is viable given income compression realities
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A generic staged return plan that works for a software engineer can be completely inapplicable to a physician or academic, leading to wasted years building toward a return that is structurally unviable

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How partner and family factors are handled in planning
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Plans own career milestones and treats partner's career as something that will work itself out after arrival, or as a secondary consideration
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats partner's career alignment as a co-equal milestone — both careers must have specific identified paths, warm networks, and role pipelines before the return trigger is pulled
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Unaligned dual careers cause household financial instability, relationship strain, and often force a reversal of the return decision after the more disruptive and costly move has already been made
